families.s: HSE human-factors design of permit-to-work systems
families.t: formal authorisation, responsible persons, signatures, high-risk work, communication, coordination, competence and risk assessment
f: A permit-to-work is a formal system stating what work is to be done, when and which parts are safe.
A responsible person should assess the work and check safety at each stage.
People carrying out the job sign to show they understand the risks and precautions.
Permits communicate between management, supervisors, operators and the people doing the work.
Written permits may be needed for hot work, vessel entry, hazardous pipework and electrical or mechanical isolation.
Permit systems help coordinate simultaneous work and avoid conflicts.
A permit-to-work does not replace a robust risk assessment.
Competence, usable procedures and effective communication are central human-factors elements of permit systems.
families.g: Formal authorisation, responsible persons, signatures, high-risk work, communication, coordination, competence and risk assessment guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE integration of human factors and ergonomics into design
families.t: control rooms, interfaces, alarms, environment, user needs, maintainability, early design and user involvement
f: Control-room, plant and equipment design can have a large impact on human performance.
Designing tasks, equipment and workstations to suit users can reduce errors, accidents and ill health.
Ergonomic design can make work safer, healthier and more productive.
Human factors should be considered as early as possible in the design process.
Human-factors expertise should be used appropriately during design.
People who understand the work process and end users should be involved.
User involvement supports operable and maintainable plant and systems.
Poor design has been identified as a root cause of serious and major accidents.

families.s: HSE ergonomic design and modification of control rooms
families.t: layout, workstations, displays, controls, interactions, lighting, acoustics, ventilation, evaluation and remote operation
f: Control-room design can significantly affect operator performance.
A work system combines people, equipment, space, environment and work organisation.
Control-room standards cover design principles and room arrangements.
Workstation layout should support the operators and tasks.
Displays and controls should support clear and reliable interaction.
Temperature, lighting, acoustics and ventilation are part of control-room design.
New control rooms should apply ergonomic design standards from the outset.
Existing rooms should be evaluated during upgrades, modifications or when performance problems are known.

families.s: HSE design review of human-system interfaces
families.t: displays, controls, feedback, consistency, information presentation, physical characteristics, functional characteristics and evaluation
f: Human-system interactions have frequently contributed to poor operator performance.
Interface design should consider both physical and functional characteristics.
Displays should present task-relevant information clearly.
Controls should be identifiable and compatible with expected operator actions.
Interface interactions should support accurate diagnosis and decision making.
Consistency and meaningful feedback can reduce confusion and error.
Interface design should be evaluated as part of control-room and work-system design.
Known interface problems should be addressed during upgrades and modifications.

families.t: fault prompting, diagnosis, relevance, defined response, timing, alarm floods, operator capability and lifecycle review
f: Optimised alarm design supports accurate and timely fault prompting and diagnosis.
Poorly designed alarm systems have contributed to major incidents.
Alarms should direct attention to plant conditions requiring timely assessment or action.
Alarms should alert, inform and guide the required operator response.
Every alarm should be useful, relevant and have a defined response.
Alarm settings should give operators enough time to respond before conditions escalate.
Alarm systems should accommodate human capabilities and limitations.
Alarm performance should be reviewed so floods, nuisance alarms and obsolete alarms do not obscure important conditions.
